zfs.title: ZFS
zfs.intro: ZFS keeps your files on one or more disks as a pool. Depending on how the disks are arranged, a pool keeps working when a disk fails, and ZFS checks every file it reads. It is not a backup: a file deleted by mistake is gone from every disk at once, unless a snapshot keeps it.

term.pool: A pool joins one or more disks into one store of space, and decides how your files survive a failed disk.
term.group: A pool is made of one or more groups of disks. Each group protects its own disks. If any group loses more disks than it can, the whole pool is lost.
term.fileSystem: A ZFS file system is a folder on a pool that you can share, with its own size limit and snapshots. All file systems on a pool share its free space.
term.poolFolder: Every pool is also a file system itself, in the folder named after the pool. It is better to keep files in file systems made on the pool.
term.volume: A volume is a part of the pool that acts as a separate disk, for virtual machines or iSCSI. This page lists volumes but does not manage them.
term.snapshot: A snapshot keeps a file system's files as they were at one moment. It takes no space at first, and grows as the files change.
term.check: A check reads every file on the pool and compares it with its copies. ZFS repairs what it finds from a good copy.

term.interface: A network interface is one way the NAS connects to a network: a network port with a cable, Wi-Fi, or one made from them (a bond, a VLAN or a bridge).
term.devicename: The NAS names each interface itself, such as enp2s0. The name stays the same unless the hardware changes.
term.ethernet: A socket for a network cable.
term.notSetUp: The NAS has this port, but it has no settings here. It gets no address, and the NAS cannot be reached through it.
term.dhcp: The router gives the NAS its address. The address can change, though most routers keep giving the same one.
term.static: You choose the address. It never changes, and no other device on the network may use it.
term.manual: The interface gets no address of this kind.
term.auto: The NAS makes its own address from what the router announces. Most home networks with IPv6 use this.
term.dhcp6: A DHCPv6 server on the network gives the NAS its address. Choose this only if your network has one.
term.netmask: Which addresses are on the same local network as the NAS. /24 means the first three numbers belong to the network, as in 192.0.2.x: 256 addresses.
term.gateway: The router the NAS sends traffic through to reach other networks and the internet. It must be on the same network as the NAS.
term.dnsnameservers: Name servers turn names such as example.org into addresses. The NAS uses them for updates, email notifications, its clock and copy jobs to named computers. They do not change how other computers find this NAS.
term.dnssearch: When the NAS looks up a short name, it also tries it with these endings, so backup can find backup.example.org.
term.mtu: The largest piece of data the NAS sends in one go, in bytes. Keep the standard size unless every device on this network uses larger (jumbo) packets.
term.wol: Lets another computer switch the NAS on through this port.
term.altmacaddress: The port's own address on the network. Changing it makes your router see a different device, so it may give the NAS a different address.
term.routemetric: When the NAS has more than one router address, it uses the one with the lower number first.
term.bond: A bond makes two or more network ports work as one. If a cable or a switch port fails, the others carry on.
term.bondprimary: The port the bond uses while it works. The others take over if it fails.
term.vlan: A VLAN is a separate network that shares a cable with others, told apart by a number, its VLAN ID. Your switch must be set up with the same number.
term.bridge: A bridge joins interfaces into one network, like a small switch inside the NAS. It is mostly used to give virtual machines and containers their own place on your network.
term.hidden: The network does not announce its name, so the NAS looks for it by name.
term.hostname: The name other computers use to find this NAS. Letters, digits and hyphens.
term.domain: The name of your network, written after the NAS's name, as in {{host}}.example.org. Leave it empty if your network has none.
term.firewall: The firewall decides which network traffic the NAS lets in and out. It checks its rules from the top and follows the first one that fits. Traffic that no rule fits is let through.
term.reject: Turn it away and tell the other computer, so it gives up at once.
term.drop: Turn it away without an answer. The other computer waits, then gives up.
term.log: Write a line in the system log, then carry on with the next rule.
term.count: Do nothing, and carry on with the next rule.
term.port: A port is a numbered door into a computer; each service has its own, such as 22 for SSH.
term.extraoptions: Options set in the classic interface. They are kept as they are.
term.proxy: A proxy is a computer that fetches web pages and files for the NAS. You need one only when your network requires it.
term.identify: The light beside the port's socket blinks, so you can find the right cable.
